course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 3
firstTopic.summary: How the Seven Years' War, British imperial reform, colonial self-government, and Enlightenment ideas set the stage for independence and the first experiments in republican government, 1754–1800.

topic.title: The American Revolution
topic.summary: How the war began, the turning points that saved the Patriot cause, and why Britain's apparent advantages were not enough to defeat the colonies.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: The first armed fighting of the Revolutionary War took place in April 1775 at
choices: Yorktown, Virginia, where a British army was trapped by American and French forces
Saratoga, New York, where a British army under General Burgoyne was forced to surrender
Trenton, New Jersey, where Washington surprised German soldiers hired by Britain
Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts, where militia clashed with British troops
questions.explanation: British troops marching to seize colonial military supplies met militia at Lexington and Concord, and the shooting began the war.
choiceExplanations: Yorktown was the last major battle, in 1781.
Saratoga was fought in 1777.
Trenton took place at the end of 1776.
British troops marching to seize colonial military supplies met militia at Lexington and Concord, and the shooting began the war.
questions.distinguisher: The Saratoga choice is close because it was an early and famous Patriot victory, but it came two years later.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following actions did the Second Continental Congress take in 1775 and 1776?
choices: It created the Continental Army, named George Washington its commander, and adopted the Declaration of Independence
It signed a peace treaty with Britain and then ratified the Constitution of the United States
It sent the Olive Branch Petition to Parliament and accepted the Coercive Acts in return for peace
It appointed Benjamin Franklin commander of the army and moved the capital from Philadelphia to Boston
questions.explanation: Congress organized the army, chose Washington, and in July 1776 declared independence after the king rejected its petition.
choiceExplanations: Congress organized the army, chose Washington, and in July 1776 declared independence after the king rejected its petition.
The peace treaty came in 1783, and the Constitution was written in 1787.
The petition was sent to the king, and Congress did not accept the Coercive Acts.
Washington was the commander, and Congress met in Philadelphia.
questions.distinguisher: The Olive Branch choice is close because the petition was real, but it went to the king and was rejected.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the Loyalists during the American Revolution?
choices: British soldiers who deserted the army and settled in the colonies to join the Patriot cause
Colonists who stayed faithful to the Crown, a substantial minority whose presence made the war partly a civil war
Colonists who supported independence but wanted a king to rule the new nation under a constitution
A small group of royal officials who had no support among the colonists and lived only in Boston
questions.explanation: A substantial minority of colonists opposed independence, and the war divided communities and families, especially in the South and parts of New York.
choiceExplanations: Loyalists were colonists who supported Britain.
A substantial minority of colonists opposed independence, and the war divided communities and families, especially in the South and parts of New York.
Loyalists wanted to remain under the Crown, not to create a new monarchy.
Loyalists lived in every colony and many were ordinary colonists.
questions.distinguisher: The royal-officials choice is close because officials were Loyalists, but the group also included many ordinary colonists.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains the importance of the Patriot victory at Saratoga in 1777?
choices: It ended the war because the British army in North America surrendered and Britain asked for peace
It gave the Americans control of the South, where they used it to force Loyalists to leave the colonies
It convinced France that the Americans could win, which led to the French alliance of 1778
It led Spain to give up Florida to the United States in return for American help against France
questions.explanation: The victory showed that the Patriots could defeat a British army, which persuaded France to ally with them and send money, supplies, and naval power.
choiceExplanations: The war continued until 1781, and the treaty was signed in 1783.
Saratoga was in New York, and the war in the South came later.
The victory showed that the Patriots could defeat a British army, which persuaded France to ally with them and send money, supplies, and naval power.
Spain joined the war against Britain later, and Florida did not pass to the United States then.
questions.distinguisher: The war-ended choice is close because Saratoga was a major victory, but the British kept fighting for years.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: George Washington contributed to the American victory mainly by
choices: keeping the Continental Army together through defeat and hardship and avoiding its destruction
winning every major battle against the British army and capturing its commanders early in the war
negotiating the alliance with France on behalf of Congress during the winter at Valley Forge
writing the Declaration of Independence and presenting it to the Second Continental Congress in 1776
questions.explanation: Washington's leadership held the army together through the winter at Valley Forge and long retreats, so the Patriots could keep fighting.
choiceExplanations: Washington's leadership held the army together through the winter at Valley Forge and long retreats, so the Patriots could keep fighting.
The Continental Army lost many battles, and Washington's strength was in keeping the army in being.
Benjamin Franklin and other diplomats negotiated the alliance in France.
Jefferson was the principal author of the Declaration.
questions.distinguisher: The battle-victories choice is close because Washington won key battles, but he lost many and his main strength was persistence.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why Britain, despite its military and financial advantages, did not defeat the Patriots?
choices: Britain's navy was destroyed in the first year of the war, and it could not ship troops to North America
Most colonists supported the Patriot cause and took up arms, so no Loyalists remained in the colonies
Britain withdrew from North America in 1776 in order to defend its holdings in India
The distance from home, the size of the colonies, and limited colonial support made it hard to hold territory
questions.explanation: British armies were thousands of miles from home, the colonies were too large to occupy, and British forces could not win enough colonial support to hold the places they captured.
choiceExplanations: The British navy stayed powerful and transported armies across the Atlantic.
Loyalists were a substantial minority throughout the war.
Britain fought in North America until 1781.
British armies were thousands of miles from home, the colonies were too large to occupy, and British forces could not win enough colonial support to hold the places they captured.
questions.distinguisher: The navy choice is close because sea power mattered, but the British navy was strong until France joined the war.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The British surrender at Yorktown in 1781 was the result of
choices: a surprise attack by Patriot militia on the British army that was sleeping in winter quarters at Valley Forge
a combined American and French army and a French fleet trapping a British army under General Cornwallis
a naval blockade of Boston Harbor by the Continental Navy, which forced British troops to leave Massachusetts
a mutiny among German soldiers hired by Britain, who refused to fight against the Patriot army
questions.explanation: French ships cut off the British by sea, and American and French troops surrounded them on land, so Cornwallis surrendered.
choiceExplanations: Valley Forge was the Patriot camp, and the surrender at Yorktown was in 1781.
French ships cut off the British by sea, and American and French troops surrounded them on land, so Cornwallis surrendered.
The British left Boston in 1776, and Yorktown is in Virginia.
Yorktown resulted from a military siege and a naval blockade.
questions.distinguisher: The Boston choice is close because Boston was an earlier blockade, but the Yorktown surrender came from French and American cooperation.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The Treaty of Paris of 1783 did which of the following?
choices: Britain kept the Northwest forts and the United States agreed to pay the taxes that it had refused before the war
France received Canada from Britain and agreed to give up its claims to the Mississippi valley
Britain recognized American independence and set the new nation's boundaries to the Mississippi River
The colonies agreed to a union under the king and to send representatives to Parliament
questions.explanation: The treaty ended the war, recognized the independence of the United States, and set boundaries from the Atlantic to the Mississippi River.
choiceExplanations: The treaty recognized independence and did not restore British taxes.
France did not receive Canada.
The treaty ended the war, recognized the independence of the United States, and set boundaries from the Atlantic to the Mississippi River.
The treaty recognized the United States as independent.
questions.distinguisher: The Northwest-forts choice is close because Britain kept forts for years, but the treaty did not restore taxes.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conclusions about the Revolutionary War is best supported by the table?
choices: The American army won every major battle between 1775 and 1783 without foreign help
Britain recognized American independence before the surrender of its army at Yorktown
The war ended in 1776 when the Declaration of Independence was adopted by Congress
Events in 1777 and 1778 brought a European ally into the war on the American side
questions.explanation: The table shows the surrender at Saratoga in 1777 followed by the Franco-American alliance in 1778.
choiceExplanations: The table lists key events, and it does not show that the Americans won every battle.
The table shows that recognition came in 1783, after Yorktown.
The table lists events through 1783.
The table shows the surrender at Saratoga in 1777 followed by the Franco-American alliance in 1778.
questions.distinguisher: The recognition choice is close because the table lists the treaty, but the treaty is dated after Yorktown.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains the importance of the event listed in the table for 1778?
choices: France forced Britain to recognize American independence by threatening an invasion of London
France supplied money, troops, and naval power that helped the Americans win at Yorktown
France ended the loyalist threat by sending its army to remove Loyalists from the colonies
France took over command of the Continental Army so that Washington could negotiate the peace
questions.explanation: The alliance gave the Patriots French money, supplies, troops, and ships, and the French fleet was decisive at Yorktown in 1781.
choiceExplanations: Britain recognized independence in 1783 after the war's end.
The alliance gave the Patriots French money, supplies, troops, and ships, and the French fleet was decisive at Yorktown in 1781.
France did not remove Loyalists.
Washington remained commander of the army.
questions.distinguisher: The recognition choice is close because the war ended with recognition, but France's role was to help win the war.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would best support the claim that European allies contributed to the American victory?
choices: Washington's army camped at Valley Forge in the winter of 1777 and 1778 and trained there
Patriot militia in Massachusetts gathered at Lexington and Concord in April 1775
French ships prevented British reinforcements and supplies from reaching Cornwallis at Yorktown
The Declaration of Independence listed grievances against the king and Parliament in July 1776
questions.explanation: French naval power cut the British off by sea at Yorktown, which is direct evidence of an ally's contribution to the victory.
choiceExplanations: Valley Forge concerned the Continental Army's own training and endurance.
This shows colonial effort and not European help.
French naval power cut the British off by sea at Yorktown, which is direct evidence of an ally's contribution to the victory.
This is a statement of colonial ideas and not evidence of European help.
questions.distinguisher: The Valley Forge choice is close because it was part of the war, but it shows American endurance and not foreign help.
